Eurasian griffon vultures (Gyps fulvus) exhibit life-history traits characteristic of long-lived, slow-reproducing scavengers. Incubation of the single egg, typically lasting around 54 days [ab = around 54 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], represents a substantial energetic investment by both parents. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling weighs a mere 200 grams [Wwb = 200 grams], a modest initial mass that belies the rapid growth trajectory required to fledge before the onset of winter. This neonatal mass is considerably less than the initial wet weight of the egg itself, which has been recorded at 252 grams [Ww0 = 252 grams], reflecting the substantial proportion of yolk and albumen that are converted into embryonic tissue during development.

Under the elevated thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods, estimated at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds in this species. The nestling period is relatively extended, with fledging—the achievement of sustained flight—occurring at approximately 113.75 days after hatching [tx = approximately 113.75 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This protracted period of parental dependency is common among large raptors and is linked to the time required for the full development of flight feathers and the musculoskeletal system necessary for soaring flight. Following fledging, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase characterized by continued growth and behavioral maturation. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the attainment of sexual maturity, is not reached until about 414 days after hatching [tp = about 414 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the extended period of somatic growth needed to reach the large adult bod at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]y size.

Adult body mass in the Eurasian griffon vulture shows marked sexual dimorphism, with females typically attaining a heavier ultimate weight. Field records indicate that the maximum adult body mass recorded for females can reach 8525 grams [Wwi = 8525 grams], while males are somewhat smaller, with an ultimate wet weight often plateauing near 8350 grams [Wwi = 8350 grams]. This difference in asymptotic mass is a common pattern among accipitrid vultures and is thought to be related to the selective pressures of female dominance at carcasses and the energetic demands of egg production. The acquisition of such a large body mass requires sustained high food intake over several years, and the transition from a juvenile to a fully grown adult is a gradual process.

The lifespan of the Eurasian griffon vulture is remarkably long, with the oldest documented individuals in the wild reaching up to 27 years [am = up to 27 years] under the thermoneutral conditions (40 °C [T = 40 °C]) typical of their Mediterranean and Asian mountain habitats. This exceptional longevity is a cornerstone of the species' life-history strategy, which prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity. Accordingly, the maximum reproductive rate is constrained; field observations show that a breeding pair typically produces a single egg per year [Ri = single egg per year]. This low annual reproductive output is balanced by a high probability of annual breeding success and extremely low adult mortality once individuals reach their prime breeding years.

First reproduction does not occur until individuals are well into their sub-adult phase, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 4 years [tR = 4 years] under the typical 40 °C [T = 40 °C] thermal regime of active metabolism. This delayed onset of breeding is a classic correlate of a "slow" life-history pace, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient foraging experience, establish a territory, and form a stable pair bond before attempting to raise offspring. The combination of a long lifespan, a low reproductive rate, a late age at first breeding, and a significant investment in each single chick renders the species particularly vulnerable to population declines from increased adult mortality. Conservation strategies thus focus intently on reducing threats from poisoning and collision with power lines.
